input.currentSkills: Survey design, customer interviews, data analysis in Excel, writing, stakeholder communication

starting_point.summary: You have direct experience with survey design, customer interviews, and stakeholder communication — three activities that commonly appear in UX research work. Your data analysis and writing experience may also carry over, though how much depends on what kind of data you have worked with and what the specific role requires.
important_unknowns: What an actual job posting would require — without one, everything here describes what commonly matters in this kind of role, not what a specific employer needs from you.
What your customer interviews and survey design were directed at — the context and methods matter for assessing how directly they transfer to a UX research setting.

What kind of data your Excel analysis covered — 'data analysis in Excel' does not establish whether you have worked with research data specifically, which affects how much that experience carries over.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied customer interviews as part of your experience.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Conducting interviews with customers may carry over to UX research, where one-on-one interviews are a commonly used method — though the framing, objectives, and analysis approach in a research context may differ from what you have done.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied survey design as part of your experience.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Survey design is a method that appears in UX research, so this experience may carry over — how directly depends on what those surveys were trying to learn and how they were structured.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied stakeholder communication as part of your four years in a B2B SaaS environment.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Communicating findings or recommendations to stakeholders is commonly relevant in UX research roles, and your existing experience in this area may transfer.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied writing as part of your experience.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Research roles often involve written deliverables such as research plans, discussion guides, and reports — your writing experience may carry over to those forms, though the specific formats would be new.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied data analysis in Excel as part of your experience.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Working with data is relevant to UX research, but what kind of data you have analyzed is not established by what you supplied — the transfer depends on whether the target role involves quantitative survey analysis or other work that overlaps with what you have done.

start_here.why_it_matters: This is a reasonable place to start because it sits at the intersection of things you already have some evidence for — interviewing, surveys, data analysis, and writing — and a capability that commonly runs through UX research work. Building here lets you develop something adjacent to your existing experience rather than starting from scratch, and it produces an artifact you can show.
start_here.current_evidence: You have experience with customer interviews, survey design, and data analysis in Excel, but what you supplied does not establish how you have synthesized or structured findings from those activities into research outputs.
start_here.gap: The difference is between conducting research activities and producing a structured analysis — identifying patterns, drawing defensible observations, and communicating what the data does and does not show.
start_here.next_move: Draft a research analysis document using interview notes or survey data you already have, or plan one using a self-contained exercise if you do not.
start_here.proof: A written document that moves from raw notes or data to organized observations and clear takeaways — even a draft version demonstrates the thinking.

next_move.primary: If you have notes or data from a past customer interview or survey you conducted, write up a short analysis: what patterns you saw, what remained unclear, and what you would have done differently with a clearer research question. If you have not done this kind of structured synthesis before, draft a research plan for a small self-contained interview study — define the question, who you would talk to, what you would ask, and how you would analyze what you heard.
next_move.why: Either version builds the synthesis and planning capability that is not yet established by what you supplied, and produces a concrete artifact you can revise or use as a portfolio starting point.
next_move.proof: A written document — either an analysis of real notes or a research plan — that you can continue developing as your understanding of the role grows.
alternatives: If you have access to a product or service you use regularly, draft a brief research plan for a usability question about it — this keeps the exercise self-contained and avoids any access or consent questions.

If your current role involves gathering customer feedback, document one recent instance in research terms: what the question was, how you gathered input, what you observed, and what a reasonable next step would have been — framing existing work in research language is a concrete step you can take without new access.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: UX research commonly begins with defining a clear, appropriately scoped research question — some roles place significant weight on this as a distinct skill.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied customer interviews and survey design, which both involve some form of question development, but what you supplied does not establish how you have defined or scoped research questions.
skill_gaps.gap: The difference between writing survey or interview questions and framing a research question that guides method choice, scope, and analysis is not established by what you supplied.
skill_gaps.next_move: Practice writing research questions for scenarios you are familiar with, then note what method each would call for and why.
skill_gaps.proof: A short written exercise pairing a research question with a method rationale — a reusable reference you can build on.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: Usability testing is a method that commonly appears in UX research roles, though how central it is varies by role and team.
skill_gaps.gap: Your supplied experience does not establish familiarity with planning, facilitating, or analyzing usability tests.
skill_gaps.next_move: Read methodological overviews of moderated and unmoderated usability testing, then draft a simple test plan for a product you use.
skill_gaps.proof: A written test plan — scenario, tasks, what you would observe and why — that shows you understand the method's structure.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: Some UX research roles require the ability to recommend a method based on the research question and constraints — not just execute a method someone else selected.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied experience with two specific methods — interviews and surveys — but what you supplied does not establish whether you have selected or justified methods in response to a defined question.
skill_gaps.gap: Having used two methods is different from being able to compare methods and explain why one fits a given question better than another.
skill_gaps.next_move: Practice writing brief rationales: given a research question, which method would you use, what would it tell you, and what would it miss?
skill_gaps.proof: A short written comparison of two methods applied to one question — a format you can reuse across different questions.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: Identifying patterns across qualitative data — interviews, open-ended responses, observational notes — is commonly relevant in UX research roles.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied customer interviews and data analysis in Excel, but neither establishes experience synthesizing qualitative research data specifically — the type and method of your past analysis is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: The difference is between working with data you have and systematically coding, grouping, and interpreting qualitative responses to answer a research question.
skill_gaps.next_move: Take a set of open-ended text responses — from a past survey or a public dataset — and practice grouping themes, labeling them, and writing one or two observations that the groupings support.
skill_gaps.proof: A documented set of labeled themes with a short written summary of what they show and what remains unclear.

skill_gaps.capability: Communicating research findings in a research format
skill_gaps.target_relevance: Presenting research findings to product, design, or business audiences is commonly part of UX research work — the format and conventions differ from general stakeholder communication.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied stakeholder communication and writing experience, which suggests familiarity with communicating to internal audiences, but does not establish experience with research-specific output formats.
skill_gaps.gap: General stakeholder communication does not establish the ability to structure a research report or readout — showing what was studied, how, what was found, and what is recommended or uncertain.
skill_gaps.next_move: Draft a short research readout using any real or practice findings you have, following the structure: question, method, observations, open questions.
skill_gaps.proof: A written or slide-based readout document — even a single example demonstrates familiarity with the format.

skill_gaps.capability: Applying ethical and consent considerations in research
skill_gaps.target_relevance: Informed consent, participant privacy, and ethical handling of research data are considerations that commonly arise when working directly with research participants.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied customer interviews, which may have involved some form of consent process, but what you supplied does not establish whether this was handled in a research context or how.
skill_gaps.gap: Research ethics and consent practices in a UX context — including what participants need to know and how their data should be handled — are not established by what you supplied.
skill_gaps.next_move: Read an overview of research ethics in a UX or applied research context, focusing on informed consent and data handling.
skill_gaps.proof: A short written summary of consent considerations you would apply to a simple interview study — shows you have engaged with the topic concretely.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying whether the role expects a formal research portfolio with documented study artifacts — screener guides, discussion guides, synthesis deliverables — or whether demonstrated experience and examples discussed in interview are sufficient.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: If a portfolio is expected, building one from your existing interview and survey work becomes a concrete pre-application task rather than an optional step.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Check several current postings for this title and look for explicit language around portfolio, work samples, or case studies in the application or requirements section.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying whether the role is embedded in a product team — working alongside designers and PMs daily — or operates as a centralized research function serving multiple teams on request.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: The embedded model tends to require faster, lighter-weight research cycles; the centralized model often involves more formal study design and longer timelines — these call for different preparation emphasis.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Look for phrases like 'partner with product and design' versus 'research team' or 'research practice' in postings, and look at org structure if the company is large enough to have public team pages.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying what level of quantitative analysis the role expects — whether basic survey analysis suffices or whether statistical fluency, significance testing, or experience with specialized analysis software is listed.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: Your Excel-based analysis may be sufficient for some roles and may fall short for others that expect more formal quantitative research methods.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Look at the required versus preferred skills sections of several postings and note whether quantitative methods or specific analytical capabilities appear there.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying whether the role expects prior experience in a specific domain — enterprise software, fintech, healthcare, consumer — or is open to candidates with transferable B2B research exposure.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: Your B2B SaaS background is relevant context, but some employers weight domain-specific user knowledge heavily in early screening.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Check whether postings list industry background as required or preferred, and look at the LinkedIn profiles of people currently in this role at target companies to see how varied their backgrounds are.

transition_tasks.task: Reframe your existing work — customer interviews, survey projects, stakeholder presentations — into research case study narratives that describe the question you were investigating, your method, what you found, and what decision it informed.
transition_tasks.why: UX Research hiring often evaluates how you think through a research problem, not just whether you have done interviews; your existing experience becomes more legible in this framing.

transition_tasks.task: Identify and connect with people currently working as UX Researchers, particularly those who came from non-design backgrounds, to learn how they describe the transition and what they wish they had prepared.
transition_tasks.why: People who made a similar move can surface role realities and unwritten expectations that postings do not capture, and may surface opportunities before they are posted.

transition_tasks.task: Update your resume and any public professional profile to foreground the research-relevant elements of your marketing work — study design, interview facilitation, insight synthesis, stakeholder communication — rather than leading with marketing outcomes.
transition_tasks.why: Hiring reviewers for a research role may not read far enough to find relevant experience if the framing signals 'marketer' before 'researcher.'

input.interests: User research, strategy and business impact

directions.why_it_connects: You supplied experience writing specs, collaborating cross-functionally with product and design, and a stated interest in strategy and business impact — these are directly relevant to how product management work is commonly described.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Product managers commonly define what gets built and why, working across engineering, design, and business stakeholders to shape roadmaps and decisions. The balance between technical depth, user understanding, and business framing varies considerably by organization and product type.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want to make decisions about what gets built without being the one who builds it — and would you find the influence-without-authority dynamic of the role satisfying day to day?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Read first-person accounts from engineers who moved into product management — search for these on personal blogs or LinkedIn posts — and look at a range of product manager job postings to see how much technical depth different organizations expect.

directions.why_it_connects: You stated an interest in user research and supplied that you ran a user interview, which gives you at least some direct exposure to the practice.
directions.what_the_work_involves: UX researchers plan and conduct studies — interviews, usability tests, surveys — to understand how people think about and use products, then synthesize findings to inform design and product decisions. The scope and methods used vary considerably by team size and maturity.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want to spend a large portion of your time in the study-design and synthesis cycle, rather than in building systems — and does the pace of research-driven work match what you are looking for?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Look for job postings for UX researcher roles and note what methods and deliverables they list, then find first-person writing from researchers about what a typical project actually looks like week to week.

directions.target_role: Developer tools or API strategy role
directions.why_it_connects: You supplied five years of backend Python and API architecture work, which is directly relevant to work focused on developer-facing products or API strategy — areas where deep technical context shapes the work.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Some organizations have roles — sometimes called developer advocate, developer experience, or technical product roles — focused on shaping or communicating APIs and tools for external or internal developers. The mix of writing, research, strategy, and building varies widely by organization.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want your technical background to remain central to your day-to-day work, or are you looking to move toward roles where it is more of a background asset than the primary focus?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Search job postings for 'developer experience,' 'API product,' and 'developer advocate' to see the range of what these roles involve, and look for first-person accounts from people in them about where they spend their time.

directions.why_it_connects: You stated an interest in strategy and business impact, and supplied experience with SQL and cross-functional collaboration — capabilities that are commonly relevant to strategy and operations work that involves data and stakeholder coordination.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Strategy and operations roles commonly involve analyzing data, framing business problems, and working across teams to drive decisions or improvements. These roles exist in many forms — inside product companies, consulting, or business operations — and the technical depth expected varies considerably.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want to work primarily on business and organizational problems rather than product or user problems — and does the idea of influencing decisions through analysis and communication, rather than through building, appeal to you?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Look at job postings for 'strategy and operations,' 'business operations analyst,' and 'go-to-market strategy' roles at companies whose products interest you, and compare what each actually lists as day-to-day responsibilities.

salary_delta.realistic_starting_salary: A career-changer landing their first PM role in 2026 without a CS background or MBA should realistically target $68–75K, not the $82K midpoint, especially at companies below 500 employees.

roi_analysis.year_3_cumulative: Assuming a $20K annual raise held and modest PM progression, you recoup transition costs in roughly 6 months and net approximately $51K more over 3 years after subtracting the $9,350 in costs.

output.negotiation_leverage: Your marketing background is genuinely differentiable — most PMs lack fluency in user messaging, go-to-market coordination, and campaign analytics, so lean hard on that in B2C or growth-focused roles where those skills directly map to PM responsibilities.
output.financial_warning: The 6-month timeline is aggressive for a career-changer with no shipped product experience; if the search stretches to 10–12 months (which is common), the income gap cost nearly doubles and payback period extends past year 1 — plan your cash reserves accordingly.

skillGaps.capability: Working with engineering on scope and feasibility
Communicating product strategy to varied audiences

first.focus: Start with user research and discovery, because it is the foundation the other gaps build on — structuring tradeoffs and defining metrics both require knowing what you learned from users and why it matters. Your marketing background gives you real exposure to audiences and messaging, which overlaps with research thinking.
first.how_youll_know: You can take a specific product or feature you already know well, write down three distinct user problems it might solve, and then explain — in plain language, without marketing framing — which one you would prioritize investigating first and why the others can wait.

then.focus: Move to structuring product decisions with tradeoffs, using what you learned in the first phase as your raw material — practice making a real or realistic decision where you have to weigh user needs against constraints you name explicitly.

later.focus: Working with engineering on scope and feasibility, and defining and tracking product metrics, can develop in parallel once the earlier two are underway — both benefit from having a concrete decision-making framework in place first. Communicating product strategy is a useful gap to address through the work itself: practice explaining decisions you have already made in the earlier phases to someone outside product.

output.plateau_note: The fix when you feel stuck: find or create one small, low-stakes product problem you can own all the way through, even outside a formal job context.
